newsitem.title: USA: Stocks extend losing streak to fourth session.
newsitem.headline: Stocks extend losing streak to fourth session.

text.p: Wall Street stocks extended their losing streak into a fourth session Monday, falling under the weight of a weak bond market and anticipation of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 16.55 points at 6,861.19.

The stock market has been on a downward slope since last Wednesday, with the blue-chip Dow index losing more than 160 points after the Fed chairman spoke in surprisingly blunt terms in his semi-annual report on the economy to the Senate of his concerns about the risks of inflation as well as the dramatic increase in stock prices.
Greenspan will make a return visit on Wednesday, this time to the House.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 13-10 on volume of 238 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Some high technology stocks rallied, shaking off recent weakness, but it was not enough to bolster the tone of the overall market.
"I think that the market is assuming a more defensive tone," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"The momentum players became disenchanted by the weakness in the high technology sector, and the question is does this mean that the overall earnings momentum in the economy is slowing? Valuations are not cheap, and you need strong earnings growth to justify them."

Metz said that the last 10 percent or 15 percent move higher in the high technology sector "was strictly trend following. Now momentum players are exiting from this area, so I think it will have more volatility."
Some technology stocks put in a steady showing, including Dow component International Business Machines Corp., which rose 1 to 144-3/4 and Ascend Communications Inc., up 1-3/4 at 54.
But Intel Corp. fell 1-1/4 to 140-5/8 while Cisco Systems Inc., the most actively traded Nasdaq issue, was down 1-1/2 at 54-1/8.

"The techs had been the real leaders in the market, but that leadership has been decimated to a certain extent," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "The better companies like Intel and Microsoft Corp. have lost their leadership role."
The tone on Monday also was set by stronger-than-forecast economic data.

January personal income rose a higher-than-forecast 0.3 percent in January compared with a revised 0.7 percent in December. Personal consumption for the month was up 0.7 percent compared with a revised 0.2 percent increase in the previous month.
The National Association of Purchasing Management said that its index of manufacturing activity rose to 53.1 in February from 52.0 in January.

"The NAPM was a disappointment," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "Not only did the overall index rise, but the closely-watched vendor deliveries and prices paid components rose, which is somewhat unsettling so far as the Fed is concerned."
He addded, "The vendor deliveries component was specifically referred to by Greenspan last week. When rising, it is often a sign of developing bottlenecks that could lead to price increases."
In the bond market, the closely watched 30-year Treasury bond lost more than half a point, raising its yield to 6.85 percent from 6.80 percent Friday.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 4.73 points at 1,304.27. The American Stock Exchange index was up 0.05 to 594.29.
